claims.text: The high-value component has localized surface damage.
The component is predisposed to hot cracking when repaired by traditional fusion welding.
Localized laser cladding can deposit a pre-alloyed hard coating on the damaged surface.
A cobalt/chromium-based alloy powder is a suitable example of the cladding material.
Controlled laser power, appropriate scanning speed, and inert shielding gas will ensure rapid melting and solidification.
Laser cladding will produce a refined, fine-grained surface microstructure.
The clad layer will contain a homogeneous dispersion of alloying elements.
The clad layer will be free of hot cracks and inherent defects.
Rapid solidification during laser cladding refines the microstructure.
Alloying elements in the deposited powder form a hard and wear-resistant surface.
Alloying elements in the deposited powder form a corrosion-resistant surface.
Laser cladding minimizes hot cracking relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The laser-clad surface will have statistically higher hardness than both a fusion-weld-repaired surface and an untreated surface.
The laser-clad surface will have significantly lower wear rate than both a fusion-weld-repaired surface and an untreated surface.
The laser-clad surface will have significantly lower corrosion rate than both a fusion-weld-repaired surface and an untreated surface.
The proposed intervention is limited to localized repair areas and the specified laser-cladding processing window.
Performance is intended to be assessed under predetermined aggressive service conditions at the component's typical operating temperature.
Cyclic mechanical loading may affect the long-term durability of the clad layer.
Variability in laser-processing parameters may affect the magnitude of the performance gains.
Failure to obtain statistically higher hardness and significantly lower wear and corrosion rates than both controls will falsify the hypothesis.
